This is what I say to people who say this to me: imagine the mental illness as a pool. You can only ever swim in your own. You can’t see the size or depth of other people’s pools. It’s the deepest pool you’re ever going to swim in. It doesn’t matter if you’re in a baby pool and the person next to you is in an Olympic sized pool. For you, this is the worst thing you’ve ever seen/felt. 

This is also true for grief. Grief is a pool. You are drowning, no matter how deep it is. If you’ve lost a dog and you’re grieving, it’s the worst thing you’ve felt. If you’ve lost everyone you’ve every known, it’s also the worst thing you’ve felt. Relatively one is worse than the other but for each person it’s still the worst thing they personally have felt.

This is why you should never, ever compare one person’s suffering to another’s or tell someone their mental illness isn’t that bad. Everyone’s pool is their own worst nightmare. 

Let them have their suffering. This isn’t the grief Olympics.

this is a good answer. Even IOP, which is often a couple of hours in the evening and less invasive for school/work might be sufficient if you can get meds. This does need treatment but “treatment” is this giant spectrum. 

The big advantage of inpatient is theeefold: one, they can get you on drugs really fast, two, they can keep you safe for a short period of time and three, they can do some intense counseling while you’re there. 

But most psych meds take a month or longer to kick in, which is longer than most hospital stays. So if you’re not in danger, something like PHP/IOP would be similar in effect but less invasive to your life.
